```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(SMSD)
# Three decimal places for numbers written into the text.
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

## What the Package Is For

SMSD ("Sequential Methods for Study Design") is for researchers who must
decide how many participants to study and do not know the population
values that a sample size formula asks for. A fixed sample size plan for
an accurate estimate needs the effect size and the variances in advance.
When those are guesses, the study ends with a confidence interval wider
than intended, or with observations it did not need. A sequential
procedure removes the guess: data are collected in stages, a stopping
rule is checked on the data in hand after each stage, and sampling ends
when the rule says the goal has been reached. The package implements
such procedures for effect sizes used throughout psychology, education,
management, marketing, and information systems, and for three kinds of
goal:

* **A narrow confidence interval** (accuracy in parameter estimation,
  AIPE): stop when the confidence interval for the effect size is no
  wider than a width you choose.
* **Minimum risk** (minimum risk point estimation, MRPE): stop when
  the cost of sampling plus the cost of estimation error is as small as
  it can be.
* **A budget**: estimate a contrast among several groups as precisely
  as a fixed budget allows, when the groups cost different amounts to
  sample.

When the population values are known well enough to fix the sample size
in advance, the sibling package DMAR has the fixed sample size planners
(`DMAR::ss_aipe_smd()` and its relatives). SMSD is for when they are
not.

## One Function to Start With

Start with `seq_aipe_smd()`, the check function for the standardized
mean difference between two groups. Every procedure in the package has
the same two parts. A pilot function (here `seq_aipe_smd_pilot()`)
returns the number of observations to collect before the stopping rule
is checked for the first time. A check function (here `seq_aipe_smd()`)
takes all the data collected so far and reports whether the rule is
met. Neither keeps any state or prints anything; the researcher collects
the data and calls the check function again after each stage.

Suppose a training program is compared with a control condition on an
engagement scale, and the aim is a 95% confidence interval for the
standardized mean difference that is no wider than 0.60. Real data
would come from participants; here two functions stand in for
recruiting them. The simulated population has means of 4.9 and 4.5 and a
standard deviation of 1 in both groups, so its standardized mean
difference is 0.4.

```{r start-pilot}
set.seed(113)
new_trained <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 4.9, sd = 1)
new_control <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 4.5, sd = 1)

m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.60)
m
trained <- new_trained(m)
control <- new_control(m)
out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
out
```

With `r m` participants per group the rule is not met: the criterion
sample size is `r attr(out, "criterion_n")` per group. The criterion is
itself an estimate and moves as data arrive, so the study does not
simply collect that many. It adds participants, here five per group at
a time, and checks again until `attr(out, "is_satisfied")` is `TRUE`.

```{r start-loop}
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  trained <- c(trained, new_trained(5))
  control <- c(control, new_control(5))
  out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
}
out
```

```{r start-values, include = FALSE}
est <- summary(out)
ci_width <- est$upper_limit - est$lower_limit
covers <- est$lower_limit <= 0.4 && 0.4 <= est$upper_limit
```

Sampling stopped at `r est$current_n` participants per group. The
interval runs from `r f3(est$lower_limit)` to `r f3(est$upper_limit)`,
a width of `r f3(ci_width)`, and
`r if (covers) "contains" else "does not contain"` the population value
of 0.4. The width never exceeds the target once the rule is met; that
part of the guarantee is exact. The coverage of the interval is an
asymptotic property, discussed under [Before Collecting
Data](#before-collecting-data).

The object returned is a data frame with columns `term` and `value`, so
any number in it can be taken out by name, and the stopping decision is
an attribute:

```{r start-object}
out$value[out$term == "smd"]
attr(out, "is_satisfied")
```

## Three Ways In

The example above is the first of the three goals: a narrow confidence
interval. The other two are run the same way, with a pilot sample and a
check after each stage.

### Minimum Risk

Suppose instead that each participant costs 4 to recruit and assess, and
that an inaccurate estimate has a price as well: the researcher would
pay 2,000 to have the estimate within 0.5 of the population value, so
one unit of squared error is priced at A = 2,000 / 0.5<sup>2</sup> =
8,000 (the construction of Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2017, p. 105).
`seq_mr_smd()` stops when the estimated total of the two costs, the
risk, is as small as it can be. The procedure targets a risk and not an
interval, so there is no confidence level.

```{r mr}
set.seed(113)
m_mr <- seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 8000, c = 4)
trained_mr <- new_trained(m_mr)
control_mr <- new_control(m_mr)
out_mr <- seq_mr_smd(trained_mr, control_mr, A = 8000, c = 4)
while (!attr(out_mr, "is_satisfied")) {
  trained_mr <- c(trained_mr, new_trained(1))
  control_mr <- c(control_mr, new_control(1))
  out_mr <- seq_mr_smd(trained_mr, control_mr, A = 8000, c = 4)
}
out_mr
```

```{r mr-values, include = FALSE}
n_mr <- out_mr$value[out_mr$term == "current_n1"]
n_best <- sqrt(8000 / (2 * 4)) * sqrt(2 + 0.4^2 / 4)
```

The pilot was `r m_mr` per group and sampling stopped at `r n_mr` per
group. Had the population value of 0.4 been known, the risk would have
been smallest at `sqrt(8000 / (2 * 4)) * sqrt(2 + 0.4^2 / 4)` =
`r round(n_best, 1)` per group (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2017, Equations
10 and 11). The procedure had to estimate that number while it sampled,
and the correction term in its stopping rule makes it take somewhat more
than the optimum.

### A Budget

Now suppose three training formats are compared, the new format against
the average of two existing ones, and an observation costs 38, 15, and
10 in the three groups. The study has 1,500 to spend. `seq_budget()`
(Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025) reports
whether sampling should continue, and `seq_budget_next()` names the
group that should receive the next observation: the one furthest below
its estimated optimal size, which depends on its weight in the contrast,
its variability, and its cost.

```{r budget}
set.seed(113)
weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5)
costs <- c(38, 15, 10)
new_score <- function(g, n) {
  rnorm(n, mean = c(52, 50, 50)[g], sd = c(9, 6, 6)[g])
}

scores <- lapply(1:3, new_score, n = seq_budget_pilot(m_0 = 10))
repeat {
  out_budget <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                           budget = 1500)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out_budget)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], new_score(g, 1))
}
out_budget
attr(out_budget, "n_per_group")
```

```{r budget-values, include = FALSE}
est_budget <- summary(out_budget)
spent <- out_budget$value[out_budget$term == "current_total_cost"]
n_budget <- attr(out_budget, "n_per_group")
covers_budget <- est_budget$lower_limit <= 2 && 2 <= est_budget$upper_limit
```

`seq_budget_next()` names only a group whose next observation the
remaining budget can pay for, so the total cost (`r spent` here) cannot
pass the budget, and it returns `NA` once sampling has ended, which is
when `attr(out_budget, "is_satisfied")` is `TRUE`. Sampling ends when
every group has reached its criterion or, as here and nearly always,
when what is left of the budget cannot pay for another observation from
a group that still needs one; the note under the result says which, and
so do the attributes `rule_met`
(`r attr(out_budget, "rule_met")` here) and `budget_exhausted`
(`r attr(out_budget, "budget_exhausted")`). The groups finished with
`r n_budget[1]`, `r n_budget[2]`, and `r n_budget[3]` observations. The
population contrast is 52 minus the average of 50 and 50, which is 2,
and the interval `r if (covers_budget) "contains" else "does not contain"`
it. The functions `decide_seq_budget_noninferiority()` and
`decide_seq_budget_equivalence()` test the contrast against a margin
once sampling has ended; see `vignette("seq-budget", package = "SMSD")`.

## The Whole Path, a Summary, and a Sentence

Three conveniences go with the check functions. They are shown here on
the first example.

`seq_path()` applies a check function to data already in hand at each
successive sample size and returns every stage in one object. All of
the data go in its second argument, as a vector for one sample or a
named list for two groups or two variables. By default it starts at the
procedure's pilot sample size and adds one observation at a time; `by =
5` reproduces the batches of the study above. (The two stage procedures
and `seq_budget()` have no path of this kind, and `seq_path()` says so
when given one.)

```{r path}
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd, list(group_1 = trained, group_2 = control),
                 width = 0.60, by = 5)
path
```

The `plot()` method draws the estimate with its confidence interval
narrowing toward the target, and the sample size against the criterion.

```{r path-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Two panels. Top: the estimated standardized mean difference and its confidence interval against the sample size per group; the interval narrows as the sample grows. Bottom: the current sample size and the criterion sample size against the sample size per group; the two meet where the stopping rule is first met."}
plot(path)
```

`summary()` condenses any check, or the stopping stage of a path, to
one row; the columns shown here are a selection.

```{r summary}
summary(path)[c("stop_n", "estimate", "lower_limit", "upper_limit",
                "criterion_n", "stages")]
```

`generics::tidy()` returns the estimate and its limits in the column
layout that DMAR uses, and `as.data.frame()` returns the plain table.

```{r tidy}
generics::tidy(out)
```

`seq_report()` writes the paragraph a methods section needs, from any
check or from a path, and carries the full reference with it.

```{r report}
seq_report(path)
```

A path shows what the rule would have said at each sample size. The
estimate a sequential study reports is the one at the first sample size
at which the rule was met, and the observations must be in the order in
which they were collected; `?seq_path` explains why.

## What the Package Contains

| Quantity estimated | Goal | Check function | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standardized mean difference | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_smd()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Coefficient of variation | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_cv()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Simple linear regression slope | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_reg_coef()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Standardized mean | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_sm()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Contrast of group means | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_c()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2018) |
| Gini index | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_gini()` | Chattopadhyay & De (2016) |
| Pearson, Kendall, or Spearman correlation | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_r()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2019) |
| Squared multiple correlation | Narrow interval | `seq_aipe_R2()` | Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay (2019) |
| Coefficient of variation | Minimum risk | `seq_mr_cv()` | Chattopadhyay & Kelley (2016) |
| Standardized mean difference | Minimum risk | `seq_mr_smd()` | Chattopadhyay & Kelley (2017) |
| Contrast across K groups with unequal costs | Budget | `seq_budget()` | Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal (2025) |
| A mean, a location, or a median | Fixed width, minimum risk, bounded risk, or bounded length | The `seq_fwd_*()`, `seq_br_*()`, and `seq_blci_*()` functions, the `seq_mr_*()` functions for a mean, and the two stage `ts_*()` functions | Mukhopadhyay & de Silva (2009) |

All of the narrow interval procedures are distribution free except the
one for the squared multiple correlation, which Kelley, Darku, and
Chattopadhyay (2019, p. 503) develop for multivariate normal data only.
Each check function has a pilot function with `_pilot` added to its
name. The classical procedures in the last row are described in
`vignette("special-cases-and-simulation", package = "SMSD")`. Two
distribution free minimum risk procedures for a mean that appeared in
development versions are held back for a later version, until they have
been checked against their source.

Many of these functions have a fixed sample size cousin in DMAR for the
case in which planning values are available (`ss_aipe_smd()`,
`ss_aipe_r()`, `ss_aipe_cv()`, `ss_aipe_reg_coef()`, `ss_aipe_sm()`,
`ss_aipe_c()`, and `ss_aipe_R2()`); each help page names its cousin.

## Before Collecting Data

The narrow interval procedures deliver the width they were asked for by
construction: once the stopping rule is met, the interval is no wider
than the target. What the theory promises about the coverage of that
interval, and about the risk of the minimum risk procedures, holds as
the sample the rule asks for grows large. With a wide target, and for
some effect sizes with a strong relationship, the rule can be met in a
sample too small for that promise. How wide is too wide depends on the
effect size, on the population value, and on the distribution of the
data.

For a standardized mean difference of 0.5 the approximation is
good at widths of 0.4 and 0.2 for normal and for right skewed data
(`?seq_aipe_smd`) and at a width of 0.8 for normal data
(`?seq_aipe_sensitivity`); with right skewed data at 0.8 the coverage
is two to three hundredths short, as a run in
`vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")` shows. For a
correlation, a regression slope, a coefficient of variation with skewed
data, and above all a squared multiple correlation with many
predictors, the approximation can be poor at targets that look
reasonable. In simulations of the procedures as shipped, with their
default settings, a 95% interval of width 0.4 contained a population
correlation of 0.4 in 0.78 of studies and a population slope of 0.5 in
0.83 with normal data, and a 95% interval of width 0.2 contained a
population coefficient of variation of 0.5 in 0.79 of studies with
lognormal data (`?seq_aipe_sensitivity`). A 95% interval of width 0.30
contained a population squared multiple correlation of 0.50 in 0.361 of
studies with 15 predictors (`?seq_aipe_R2`). Each help page reports what
was measured for its procedure and what helps: a narrower target, a
larger pilot sample, or both.

The classical procedures whose confidence level is asymptotic call for
the same care. The distribution free two stage interval for a mean, with
its default first stage of 30 observations and a narrow target, covers a
normal mean with probability
`r formatC(2 * pt(qnorm(0.975), df = 29) - 1, format = "f", digits = 3)`
(the probability that a *t* variable with 29 degrees of freedom falls
between the two normal quantiles of a 95% interval), and in simulations
it contained the population mean in 0.876 of studies with lognormal
data, where 0.95 was asked for (`?ts_fwd_dfr_mean`).
<!-- not from a help page: 29 -->

The remedy is to look before sampling. The `*_sensitivity()` functions
run a procedure from pilot to stopping many times on simulated data
with a known population value and summarize the final sample size and
the coverage or the risk. Every narrow interval procedure has one (for
the correlation it studies the Pearson coefficient), and so do
`seq_mr_cv()`, `seq_mr_smd()`, and `seq_budget()`. For the study of the
first example, with a population value of 0.4, a target width of 0.60,
and a check after every five participants per group:

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.4, width = 0.60, G = 200,
                                 seed = 113, batch = 5)
sens
```

```{r sensitivity-values, include = FALSE}
cov_sens <- sens$value[sens$term == "coverage"]
se_sens <- sqrt(cov_sens * (1 - cov_sens) / 200)
```

A study like the one above should expect to end with about
`r round(sens$value[sens$term == "mean_n"])` participants per group.
The coverage row rests on only 200 replications, used here to keep the
vignette quick: its Monte Carlo standard error is `r f3(se_sens)`, so
`r f3(cov_sens)` is not evidence of a shortfall. (In larger runs with
normal data and a population value of 0.5, coverage was 0.952 at a
width of 0.4, from 6,000 replications, and 0.95 at a width of 0.8;
`?seq_aipe_smd` and `?seq_aipe_sensitivity`.) A design that will be
reported deserves 10,000 replications, which can take from minutes to an
hour or more at a narrow target, so time a call with a small `G` first.
`vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")` explains each row.

One more thing can appear in a check. In a small sample the variance
estimate that a stopping rule needs can come out zero or negative. The
check then reports the rule as not met, with a note that says why, and
sampling continues; `vignette("seq-aipe-smd", package = "SMSD")` shows
what that looks like.

## Where to Go Next

* `vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package = "SMSD")`: one
  study from plan to report, in detail.
* `vignette("seq-aipe-smd", package = "SMSD")` and
  `vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD")`: the narrow
  interval procedures for the standardized mean difference, the
  correlation coefficients, and the squared multiple correlation.
* `vignette("mrpe-cv", package = "SMSD")` and
  `vignette("mrpe-smd", package = "SMSD")`: minimum risk point
  estimation.

  procedure and its tests.
* `vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")`: studying a
  design before collecting data.
* `vignette("special-cases-and-simulation", package = "SMSD")`: the
  classical procedures for a mean.
